name: Monotrophic diet

card.summary: Eating a single food or food type for a period, which people use to lose weight quickly and lean out, with a visible slimmer look.
card.note: Experts describe nutrient-deficiency and disordered-eating risks.

quick.overview:
A monotrophic, or mono, diet means eating only one food or food group for all meals for a set period, commonly one to two weeks. People use it to lose weight fast, which can make the face and body look leaner.

Variants include all-potato, all-egg, all-milk, all-fruit and meat-only (the lion diet). Weight loss comes largely from reduced calories and water loss. No large controlled trials exist; dietitians view it as unsustainable.
quick.how: Practitioners pick one food, eat it as their only meal, and often drink only water, usually for days to a couple of weeks before returning to varied eating.
quick.risks: Experts cite nutrient deficiencies, fatigue, constipation, muscle loss and weight regain, with higher risk for pregnant people, people with diabetes, and people with eating disorders. Some experts say pursuing a mono diet can signal a developing eating disorder.

lead: A monotrophic diet is a fad diet in which a person eats only one food or one type of food. People follow it for crash dieting, as the start of an elimination diet, or as an extreme form of alternative medicine [1].

Its appearance rationale is rapid weight loss, which proponents hope will slim the face and waist, plus claims of reduced bloating and cravings [2]. Examples include the lion diet of beef, salt and water promoted by Jordan Peterson, Piero di Cosimo's reported boiled eggs, Bernarr Macfadden's 1920s milk diet, and potato diets such as Chris Voigt's 2010 two-month potato run [1].

angle.text: People use mono diets for quick fat and water loss over days to weeks, aiming for a leaner look.

paras: Variants use a single food (potato, apple, banana, yogurt) or food group (fruit, vegetables, meat, dairy), with water as the only drink [2]. The meat-only lion diet is a stricter form of the carnivore diet [1].

Single-food eating has been attributed to individuals such as painter Piero di Cosimo and the eccentric George Sitwell [1]. Macfadden popularized a milk diet in the 1920s [1]. Online influencers and wellness retreats have contributed to its modern spread [2].
Proponents claim rapid weight loss, simpler digestion, mental clarity, fewer food decisions and reduced cravings [2].

Dietitians and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics are described as regarding it as an unsustainable fad, and experts advise balanced diets or at most one to two days under supervision [2]. Reported risks include nutrient deficiency, electrolyte problems, muscle loss, gallstones from rapid loss, and weight regain [2]. Long-term risks listed include anaemia, osteoporosis and malnutrition [1].
No studies found. Evidence is limited to anecdotal and self-experiment accounts, such as a 60-day potato-only self-experiment reporting short-term weight loss and vitamin deficiencies [2].

timeline.event: Bernard Moncriff's book describes a beef-and-milk regimen [2].
Bernarr Macfadden popularizes a milk diet [1].
Chris Voigt eats potatoes for two months [1].
Penn Jillette begins a weight-loss effort with two weeks of potatoes [1].
